title: Symmetrical surface-tension pull sets heliozoan filaments radially

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Symmetrical surface-tension pull sets heliozoan filaments radially

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Fluid surface protoplasm creeps up the stiff axial filaments of a heliozoan such as Actinophrys, and because this surface-tension pull is symmetrical around each filament the filaments are set normal to the cell surface, radiating from the centre; closely spaced filaments produce honeycomb-like depressions between them.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Since the attraction exercised by this surface tension is symmetrical around the filament, the latter will be pulled equally in all directions; in other words it will tend to be set normally to the surface of the sphere, that is to say radiating directly outwards from the centre.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter V, “The Forms of Cells”; topic “Heliozoa and radiating filaments”. Scope: Heliozoa and radiolarians with radiating axopodia or spicules

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch05-22: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.51

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The angular and curvature consequences are measurable, but mapping Thompson's surface-tension attraction to modern cell mechanics is not unique. Existing imagery can assess morphology, while distinguishing tension from cytoskeletal anchoring generally requires perturbation data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure axopod angles to the local membrane, filament spacing, and intervening membrane curvature in microscopy images, then test whether radiality and honeycomb depressions track the predicted symmetric surface pull.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Static images do not measure surface tension or establish causation.

Relevant taxa are sparsely represented in public image archives.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The geometric half, radial filaments and honeycomb depressions, is measurable wherever Actinophrys-type cells have been imaged in three dimensions. Public coverage is a handful of classical and modern studies, not a downloadable survey of heliozoa and radiolarian axopodia. Distinguishing a surface-film tug from microtubule anchoring needs those ultrastructures, which exist only piecemeal.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure axopod angles to the cell surface and the spacing of surface depressions, and compare that geometry with the ultrastructure of the filament. Radial filaments normal to the surface would match the stated outcome; filaments positioned by an internal axoneme, or oblique filaments with the same surface film, would count against surface-tension pull as the placing mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A radial arrangement is expected under several cytoskeletal rules, so static angles do not isolate symmetrical surface-tension pull.

Heliozoan electron micrographs and live orientations are scattered through papers rather than gathered in one public morphometric table.
